title: Fixed-point neural samplers on discrete spaces

paper.title: Fixed-point neural samplers on discrete spaces
paper.abstract:
Abstract Sampling from discrete, unnormalized distributions without access to data is a
challenging problem. Neural samplers offer a promising approach by training
generative models from density evaluations directly. Despite recent progress,
existing discrete neural samplers are prone to mode collapse, come without
convergence guarantees when trained via fixed-point iterations, and are often tied
to a specific reference process such as masked or uniform diffusion. In this work,
we introduce Discrete Gibbs Iterative Neural Sampler, a fixed-point neural sampler that addresses these limitations,
enabling efficient, scalable learning, substantially reducing mode collapse in
practice. Our framework builds on masked diffusion and also extends to transport
between pairs of distributions. We demonstrate that the resulting method scales
effectively to high-dimensional systems, supports amortized sampling across
different conditions, and enables accurate estimation of alloy phase diagrams.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Sampling from discrete distributions is a fundamental problem in physics, chemistry, and machine learning, yet remains computationally intractable in many settings of practical interest. Consider configurations x = ( x 1 , … , x D ) ∈ 𝒳 = 𝒜 D x=(x^{1},\ldots,x^{D})\in\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{A}^{D} , where D D is the number of sites and each x d x^{d} takes values in a finite alphabet 𝒜 \mathcal{A} . Given an unnormalized density p ~ : 𝒳 → ℝ \tilde{p}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} , the target distribution is π ⁡ ( x ) = p ~ ​ ( x ) Z , Z = ∑ x ∈ 𝒳 p ~ ​ ( x ) . \pi(x)=\frac{\tilde{p}(x)}{Z},\qquad Z=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\tilde{p}(x). (1) This formulation encompasses spin configurations, protein sequences, and distributions over solutions to combinatorial problems. Although the unnormalized density of an individual configuration can be evaluated, the exponentially large state space generally precludes enumeration. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) ( Brooks et al., 2011 ) avoids evaluating Z Z , but can mix prohibitively slowly when high probability regions are separated by high energy barriers or narrow transition pathways. The continuous counterpart of this problem has seen substantial progress through neural samplers , generative models trained on a target distribution specified by its energy function without precurated data. Boltzmann generators pioneered this idea for molecular equilibrium sampling with normalizing flows but suffered from scaling issues to systems of practical interest ( Noé et al., 2019 ) . More recent methods ( Blessing et al., 2026c ; Havens et al., 2026 ) have developed scalable training procedures for diffusion models based on fixed-point iterations by exploiting gradient information of the target density combined with efficient reuse of evaluated configurations. These advances have enabled neural samplers to tackle realistic materials systems, with substantial improvements in efficiency compared to classical Monte Carlo methods ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) . Algorithm 1 DIG-IN Input: target p ~ \tilde{p} , initial model, training loss; buffer size B B , refill size b b , minibatch size m m , inner steps K K , ESS fraction ξ \xi . Repeat until training is complete: 1: Generate b b samples from current sampler, and append them to buffer. 2: Store their sample and importance weights w w ; keep the newest B B buffer samples. 3: for k = 1 , … , K k=1,\ldots,K do 4: Draw m m buffer entries uniformly. 5: Mask sites randomly for each sample. 6: Calculate Gibbs labels for unmasked sites. 7: Choose ν ⋆ \nu^{\star} by ESS control ( ξ \xi ). 8: Update model with w ¯ \bar{w} -weighted cross-entropy loss with Gibbs label. 9: end for Return: the trained sampler. Figure 1: DIG-IN iteration. One training iteration consists of data collection, importance weight smoothing using ESS control, and parameter updates using a weighted cross-entropy loss. In this work, we introduce Discrete Gibbs Iterative Neural Sampler (DIG-IN), a fixed-point neural sampler that is inspired by the principles underlying the successes of continuous neural samplers. At the core of our approach are Gibbs labels , i.e., normalized distributions over single-site perturbations of a discrete configuration that provide a discrete analogue of gradient. In summary, DIG-IN i) incorporates these Gibbs labels which provide a strong learning signal and help to avoid mode collapse ( Section 3.1 ), ii) achieves a balance between variance and bias through tempered importance weighting, and enjoys convergence guarantees for certain setting ( Section 3.2 ), and iii) is extendable to allow for a transport between any two pairs of distributions, whereas existing discrete constructions are often tied to specific reference distributions or corruption processes ( Section 3.3 ). Experiments on Ising and Potts models show that DIG-IN is the only method that avoids mode collapse in the ordered phase while giving accurate ln ⁡ Z \ln Z estimates. It scales to amortized sampling over thermodynamic conditions on lattices with up to D = 2500 D=2500 sites, and it accurately recovers the phase diagrams of two alloy systems ( Section 5 ).

3 Discrete Gibbs Iterative Neural Sampler
sections.text: Here, we introduce Discrete Gibbs Iterative Neural Sampler (DIG-IN). We first derive Gibbs labels from single-site energy differences and show that they provide a lower-variance training signal for the masked denoiser ( Section 3.1 ). Since target samples are unavailable, we then turn this into a fixed-point iteration on self-generated samples, corrected by ESS-tempered importance weights, and state convergence analysis ( Section 3.2 ). Finally, we extend the construction beyond masked diffusion to general discrete interpolants between two distributions ( Section 3.3 ).

sections.heading: 3.3 Beyond masked diffusion
sections.text: We next extend the construction beyond masked diffusion to general discrete interpolants. Unlike the masked case where we have specified the masking process and learn the unmasking process with a single conditional predictor, for a general interpolant, however, we seek two transition dynamics, a forward and a backward process, that are exact time reversals of one another. This mirrors the role of stochastic interpolants ( Albergo et al., 2025 ) in continuous spaces, where a prescribed probability path can be associated with mutually time-reversed forward and backward dynamics. We proceed in two steps. First, we establish a general discrete interpolant construction that jointly defines forward and backward generators satisfying the time-reversal relation. We then show how the quantities defining these generators can be learned directly from endpoint energy functions, extending the Gibbs-supervision principle developed above beyond masked diffusion. We include detailed derivation in Appendix C and present experimental verification in Section F.1 .

sections.heading: Neural samplers on discrete spaces.
sections.text: Discrete neural samplers include AR models ( Wu et al., 2019 ; Nicoli et al., 2020 ) , GFlowNets ( Bengio et al., 2021 ; Malkin et al., 2022 ) , and CTMCs including LEAPS, MDNS, PDNS, Discrete ASBS, JANUS ( Holderrieth et al., 2025a ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026b ; Guo et al., 2026a ; Blessing et al., 2026b ) . Ours combines Gibbs soft-label supervision with tempered importance weighting, achieving a stable and scalable training and also mitigating mode collapsing.

sections.heading: Discrete interpolant and flow models.
sections.text: Our method supports construction for general interpolants between two arbitrary distributions. Discrete flow and generator matching also support learning dynamics between general distributions ( Gat et al., 2024 ; Holderrieth et al., 2025b ) . However, they typically do not learn a pair of time-reversed forward and backward dynamics. Recently, He et al. (2026) develop a framework for learning mutually time-reversed forward and backward dynamics. However, they all consider data-based training, while our method learns the local conditional distribution and temporal potential from endpoint energies. Appendix D provides a more detailed discussion on the related works.

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We perform several experiments on the Ising and Potts lattice spin models at different stages of the phase transition ( Section 5.1 ). Next, we test our method on larger lattices, where we train an amortized sampler that is conditioned on two thermodynamic parameters ( Section 5.2 ). Lastly, we consider two alloys, where the quantity of interest is a phase diagram ( Section 5.3 ). We refer to Appendix E for details on the experimental setup and to Appendix F for further experiments, including a component ablation and a bridge between two Boltzmann distributions.

sections.heading: 5.3 Alloy phase diagrams
sections.text: Mapping the phase diagram of an alloy requires sampling atomic configurations across a plane of chemical conditions ( T , Δ ​ μ ) (T,\Delta\mu) . We train one amortized sampler per alloy, conditioned on ( T , Δ ​ μ ) (T,\Delta\mu) , and compare DIG-IN with FrOGS ( Min et al., 2026 ) , which places a conditioned autoregressive prior ( Du et al., 2026b ) in front of learned LEAPS transport. The systems are those of Damewood et al. (2022) and Min et al. (2026) , i.e., Ag–Pd on a 5 × 5 × 5 5{\times}5{\times}5 fcc cell ( D = 125 D=125 ), with a single miscibility gap, and Cu–Au on an 8 × 4 × 4 8{\times}4{\times}4 cell ( D = 128 D=128 ), with three ordered phases. The energy is a DFT-fitted cluster expansion and the target is semi-grand canonical over T ∈ [ 200,900 ] T\in[200,900] K and Δ ​ μ ∈ [ − 0.4 , 0.4 ] \Delta\mu\in[-0.4,0.4] eV. Each method trains one model per system for 60k steps on the same energy, grid and conditioning distribution with 3 seeds, and draws 5000 samples at each of the grid points. Phase diagrams are computed using log ⁡ Z ⁡ ( T , Δ ​ μ ) \log Z(T,\Delta\mu) estimates paired with the common-tangent construction of Min et al. (2026) . For further details see Sections E.3.1 , E.3.2 and E.3.3 . DIG-IN leads on every quantity measured, on both systems ( Figure 3 ). Its free energy is one to two orders of magnitude closer to the reference and its ESS \ESS is significantly higher. Moreover, DIG-IN correctly recovers the phase boundaries without adding spurious ones on both systems. In contrast, FrOGS fails at finding all phase boundaries and adds several spurious ones.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced DIG-IN, a fixed-point neural sampler for discrete, unnormalized distributions. DIG-IN uses Gibbs labels which turn local energy differences into a soft target for the masked denoiser that has the same optimum as the one-hot objective but lower variance. Since target samples are unavailable, DIG-IN trains on self-generated configurations and corrects the resulting bias with importance weights tempered under ESS control. Assuming exact sampling and exact population fitting, this iteration provably converges to the target: for a fixed reveal order at any tempering exponent, and for arbitrary reveal orders once the tempering exponent is sufficiently close to one. The same Gibbs supervision carries over from masked diffusion to general discrete interpolants between two distributions. Empirically, DIG-IN avoids mode collapse in the ordered phase of the Ising and Potts models while also giving accurate ln ⁡ Z \ln Z estimates, successfully scales to lattices with up to D = 2500 D=2500 sites when amortizing over thermodynamic conditions, and recovers the phase diagrams of Ag–Pd and Cu–Au alloys.

sections.heading: Limitations and future work.
sections.text: Despite lowering or matching the computational costs compared to most baselines, Gibbs labels requires computing single-site energy differences. For local energies such as lattice models and cluster expansions, this table costs about one energy evaluation. For a black-box energy, however, it requires D ⁡ ( N − 1 ) + 1 D(N-1)+1 evaluations per configuration. This motivates cheaper label estimators, for instance by subsampling sites. While we establish convergence guarantee for the certain setting of our algorithm, it does not cover the practical setting in our experiments all. Moreover, the benefit and extension of general interpolants are worth further studying. The broader applications of discrete samplers in biology and chemistry are left as future work.

sections.heading: Appendix B Convergence of DIG-IN
sections.text: This section studies an idealized population version of the masked training loop, designed to isolate the dynamics of the fixed-point iteration from finite-sample and optimization errors. We replace the neural network by an unrestricted table of positive categorical heads g g , one for every training-supported context. The state space is finite, the target distribution p p is strictly positive, and both the sampling distribution and the tempered training objective are evaluated exactly. Each outer iteration returns the exact population minimizer rather than the result of finite neural-network optimization. The reveal-order law ρ \rho is fixed and independent of the generated values. Training masks are drawn independently of both the endpoint and the generating order, and their support covers every predictor head that can be queried during generation. Under these assumptions, one outer iteration is the deterministic map g ↦ Φ ν ​ ( g ) g\mapsto\Phi_{\nu}(g) given contextwise by Equation 39 . The analysis below establishes when repeated application of this map converges to the target heads.

sections.heading: Neural samplers on discrete spaces.
sections.text: Early work on discrete neural samplers uses autoregressive models ( Wu et al., 2019 ; Pan et al., 2021 ; Hibat-Allah et al., 2021 ; Nicoli et al., 2020 ; McNaughton et al., 2020 ; Białas et al., 2022 ; Białas et al., 2023 ; Sanokowski et al., 2023 ) , with subsequent work developing architectural refinements ( Biazzo, 2023 ; Del Bono et al., 2025 ; Białas et al., 2026 ) . These models provide explicit generation probabilities and can be trained through variational objectives ( Wu et al., 2019 ; Nicoli et al., 2020 ) . GFlowNets instead learn generation policies from unnormalized rewards ( Bengio et al., 2021 ; Malkin et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ; Jain et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) , while variational annealing and diffusion samplers address combinatorial optimization and statistical physics ( Sanokowski et al., 2024 ; Sanokowski et al., 2025 ) . Recent CTMC-based approaches include locally equivariant rate models ( Holderrieth et al., 2025a ; Ou et al., 2025b ) , importance-weighted energy-based generator matching with bootstrapping ( Woo et al., 2025 ) , optimal-control approaches to masked diffusion ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026a ) , and discrete adjoint matching or off-policy bridge learning ( Guo et al., 2026b ; Carter et al., 2026 ) . Applications include sampling disordered materials and alloys ( Damewood et al., 2022 ; Du et al., 2026b ; Blessing et al., 2026b ; Min et al., 2026 ) , with related work also investigating enhanced sampling ( Du et al., 2026a ) . Among masked energy-based samplers, MDNS trains with importance-weighted denoising cross entropy ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) . Our method retains the cross-entropy objective but replaces one-hot reconstruction targets with Gibbs soft labels, combining this supervision with tempered importance weighting. This use of local energy information is motivated by continuous neural samplers, including adjoint Schrödinger bridge sampling, neural flow samplers, and bridge matching samplers, which incorporate energy-gradient information into their learning objectives ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Blessing et al., 2026c ) . Single-site energy differences play a related informational role in discrete spaces, without requiring a differentiable extension of the energy, and are also exploited by discrete ASBS ( Guo et al., 2026b ) . Our construction converts these local comparisons into categorical supervision. This local conditional-matching objective is also related to distribution-based target concrete score matching ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Masked diffusion models.
sections.text: Discrete diffusion with uniform or masking noise ( Hoogeboom et al., 2021 ; Austin et al., 2021 ) has been formulated in continuous time ( Campbell et al., 2022 ) , through ratio estimation ( Meng et al., 2022 ; Sun et al., 2023 ; Lou et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) , and through flow or generator matching along general probability paths ( Campbell et al., 2024 ; Gat et al., 2024 ; Shaul et al., 2025 ; Holderrieth et al., 2025b ) . For masking processes, training reduces to a weighted cross-entropy objective for conditional categorical predictions ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) . Under value-independent masking, the exact clean-symbol conditional does not depend on time once the revealed context is given ( Ou et al., 2025a ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . Masked models also admit an any-order autoregressive interpretation ( Uria et al., 2014 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2022 ; Shih et al., 2022 ) , while masked parallel decoding predates these diffusion formulations ( Ghazvininejad et al., 2019 ; Chang et al., 2022 ; Bond-Taylor et al., 2022 ) . Trained from data, masked diffusion has been developed for language and protein modeling ( Nie et al., 2025a ; Gong et al., 2025 ; Nie et al., 2025b ; Ye et al., 2025 ; Arriola et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . Related advances include guidance ( Nisonoff et al., 2025 ; Schiff et al., 2025 ) , correctors and remasking ( Zhao et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) , reveal-order planning ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Peng et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) , and energy-based or uniform-state variants ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Sahoo et al., 2025 ) . Our setting differs from these data-trained constructions: the target is specified through an unnormalized energy, without access to target-distributed training samples. We nevertheless exploit the same conditional-generation structure. For a sampled single-site reveal order, the conditional generation probability is a tractable product of categorical prediction probabilities ( Hoogeboom et al., 2022 ) . This permits exact importance weights on an augmented space that includes the generation path and its reveal order. It does not imply that the marginal probability of a random-order model, obtained by summing over reveal orders, is tractable.

sections.heading: Discrete interpolant and flow models.
sections.text: Discrete flow matching and generator matching learn transition dynamics along general interpolant paths ( Gat et al., 2024 ; Holderrieth et al., 2025b ) . However, they do not consider constructing time-reversal forward and backward between two arbitrary distributions. He et al. (2026) develop a general framework for learning such dynamics from endpoint interpolants. However, all these models only consider data-based training, while our interpolant framework makes use of the Gibbs label for efficient energy-based training.

sections.heading: DIG-IN .
sections.text: A masked interpolant. The sampler reveals one site per network evaluation in a uniformly random order, D D evaluations per draw, so the proposal density of every draw is exact. Training runs the fixed-point loop: every 100 gradient steps the EMA model draws 512 configurations into a replay buffer of 2048, each stored with its exact table of single-site energy differences. The denoiser is trained by soft cross-entropy onto the Gibbs labels of the buffered endpoints at freshly masked copies of them, with the labels damped toward the EMA model’s prediction ( η = 0.1 \eta=0.1 ) and the per-endpoint losses weighted by importance weights tempered to an ESS \ESS of 0.8 within each training batch. Batch 128, learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , EMA decay 0.995, gradient clipping at 1.0.

sections.heading: MDNS.
sections.text: The masked diffusion neural sampler ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , run in the same codebase with the same interpolant, backbone, sampler, buffer and optimizer as DIG-IN . It is trained by cross-entropy onto the endpoint’s own token rather than a heat-bath label, weighted by the full self-normalized importance weights, without tempering and without damping.

sections.heading: PDNS.
sections.text: The proximal diffusion neural sampler ( Guo et al., 2026a ) : MDNS with its importance weights tempered to an ESS \ESS of 0.8 within each training batch, the same rule as DIG-IN . Labels are hard and there is no damping, so PDNS differs from DIG-IN in exactly the label and the damping, and from MDNS in exactly the tempering.

sections.heading: DASBS.
sections.text: The discrete adjoint Schrödinger bridge sampler ( Guo et al., 2026b ) : a time-conditioned controller and a time-free corrector, both on the shared backbone, over a uniform reference CTMC with a log-linear noise schedule ( γ = 1 \gamma=1 , α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 ). The two are trained in alternating stages of Bregman matching, 400 controller steps and then 200 corrector steps; the controller regresses onto the target’s single-site score ratios at the endpoint, which needs the energy-difference table. Each batch of 128 endpoints is replicated 8 times, the buffer of 2048 is refreshed with 512 rollouts every 20 steps, and a draw takes 100 steps. Learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} , EMA decay 0.9999. With memory, the path weights give ln ⁡ Z \ln Z only at convergence and no importance weights, so its | Δ ​ ln ⁡ Z | |\Delta\ln Z| and ESS \ESS are not reported; the memoryless variant drops the corrector and has unbiased path weights.

sections.heading: LEAPS.
sections.text: LEAPS ( Holderrieth et al., 2025a ) learns a CTMC that transports the uniform distribution to the target along the annealed path ρ t ∝ e − t ​ β ​ E \rho_{t}\propto e^{-t\beta E} , with a locally equivariant rate network (20 channels, kernels 3, 5, 7 and 9) and a free-energy MLP (hidden width 200), trained on the squared residual of the Kolmogorov forward equation at buffered trajectory states. We use training rollouts of 128 walkers every 20 steps, fill a buffer of 50 rollouts, and each loss batch holds 128 states. Rates are clamped at 10. Learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , decayed by 0.995 every 1000 steps. Importance weights follow from the discrete Jarzynski equality.

sections.text: Each run trains on one 80 GB H100 for 150k steps. Table 3 reports the training time and the number of energy calls during training, counted per configuration. A method calls the target for two things: the energy E ⁡ ( σ ) E(\sigma) of a configuration, for its importance weight or the annealed path, and the table of single-site energy differences { E ⁡ ( σ d ← n ) − E ⁡ ( σ ) } d ≤ D , n ≤ q \{E(\sigma^{d\leftarrow n})-E(\sigma)\}_{d\leq D,\,n\leq q} , which DIG-IN needs for its heat-bath labels and DASBS and LEAPS for their training targets. For the lattice models the energy is local, and the whole table follows from one neighbour-count pass at about the cost of a single energy evaluation, so we count it as one call. For a target that is only available as a black box, the table needs the energy of every configuration that differs from σ \sigma in one site, that is D ⁡ ( q − 1 ) + 1 D(q-1)+1 energy evaluations instead of 1; the black-box column counts the same runs at this rate, 626 626 calls per table for the Ising model and 513 513 for the Potts model. Neural samplers offer a promising approach by training generative models from density evaluations directly. Despite recent progress, existing discrete neural samplers are prone to mode collapse, come without convergence guarantees when trained via fixed-point iterations, and are often tied to a specific reference process such as masked or uniform diffusion. In this work, we introduce Discrete Gibbs Iterative Neural Sampler, a fixed-point neural sampler that addresses these limitations, enabling efficient, scalable learning, substantially reducing mode collapse in practice. Although the unnormalized density of an individual configuration can be evaluated, the exponentially large state space generally precludes enumeration. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) ( Brooks et al., 2011 ) avoids evaluating Z Z , but can mix prohibitively slowly when high probability regions are separated by high energy barriers or narrow transition pathways. The continuous counterpart of this problem has seen substantial progress through neural samplers , generative models trained on a target distribution specified by its energy function without precurated data. These advances have enabled neural samplers to tackle realistic materials systems, with substantial improvements in efficiency compared to classical Monte Carlo methods ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) . In this work, we introduce Discrete Gibbs Iterative Neural Sampler (DIG-IN), a fixed-point neural sampler that is inspired by the principles underlying the successes of continuous neural samplers. At the core of our approach are Gibbs labels , i.e., normalized distributions over single-site perturbations of a discrete configuration that provide a discrete analogue of gradient. Discrete neural samplers include AR models ( Wu et al., 2019 ; Nicoli et al., 2020 ) , GFlowNets ( Bengio et al., 2021 ; Malkin et al., 2022 ) , and CTMCs including LEAPS, MDNS, PDNS, Discrete ASBS, JANUS ( Holderrieth et al., 2025a ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026b ; Guo et al., 2026a ; Blessing et al., 2026b ) . Ours combines Gibbs soft-label supervision with tempered importance weighting, achieving a stable and scalable training and also mitigating mode collapsing. Discrete interpolant and flow models. Our method supports construction for general interpolants between two arbitrary distributions. Discrete flow and generator matching also support learning dynamics between general distributions ( Gat et al., 2024 ; Holderrieth et al., 2025b ) . However, they typically do not learn a pair of time-reversed forward and backward dynamics. Recently, He et al. (2026) develop a framework for learning mutually time-reversed forward and backward dynamics. However, they all consider data-based training, while our method learns the local conditional distribution and temporal potential from endpoint energies.
